patterns: how do I clean a cut
responses: For a small cut or scrape: wash your hands, rinse the area under clean running water, gently remove visible dirt, then cover it with a clean bandage. Change the bandage if it gets wet or dirty. Get urgent help now if bleeding will not stop with firm pressure, the cut is deep or gaping, or something is stuck in it.

For a small burn, cool it under cool running water for 20 minutes as soon as you can. Remove rings or tight items nearby before swelling starts. Cover loosely with a clean non-fluffy dressing. Do not use ice, butter, or toothpaste. Get urgent help for a large, deep, white or charred burn, a chemical or electrical burn, or a burn on the face, hands, feet, genitals, or a major joint.

Bruises often improve with time. Rest the area and use a cold pack wrapped in cloth for up to 15–20 minutes at a time during the first day or two. Do not put ice directly on skin. Get medical advice if bruising is very large, very painful, happens without a clear injury, or you also feel unwell or take blood-thinning medicine.

For a possible sprain or strain, protect and rest the area, use a cold pack wrapped in cloth for 15–20 minutes at a time, and raise it when comfortable. Gentle support can help if it is not tight or numb. Seek urgent assessment if you cannot put weight on it, it looks crooked, there is severe swelling or numbness, or the pain is worsening.

patterns: how do I stop a nose bleed
responses: For a nosebleed, sit up and lean slightly forward. Pinch the soft part of the nose just below the bony bridge continuously for 10–15 minutes, and breathe through the mouth. Do not tilt the head back. Get urgent help if bleeding is heavy, follows a significant head injury, causes weakness or trouble breathing, or has not stopped after 20 minutes of steady pressure.

A small head bump can often be watched closely. Rest, use a cold pack wrapped in cloth for short periods, and have someone check in on the person. Get emergency help now for loss of consciousness, repeated vomiting, seizure, confusion, worsening headache, weakness, unusual behavior, or fluid/blood from the nose or ears. If you are unsure, it is safer to seek medical advice.

patterns: how do I remove a splinter
tiny piece of glass in skin
responses: For a small, easy-to-see splinter, wash your hands and the area, then use clean tweezers to pull it out in the same direction it entered. Wash again and cover if needed. Do not dig deeply. Get medical help for glass, a deep splinter, one near the eye, signs of infection, or if you cannot remove it easily.

For a typical insect bite or sting, wash the area and use a cold pack wrapped in cloth for comfort. If a bee stinger is visible, gently scrape it sideways away with a card rather than squeezing it. Get emergency help now for trouble breathing, swelling of the lips, tongue, or throat, faintness, widespread hives, or repeated vomiting.

Choking can be an emergency. If the person cannot speak, cough, or breathe, call local emergency services now and follow their instructions. If they can cough strongly, encourage coughing and stay with them. Do not put fingers in their mouth unless you can clearly see and easily remove the object.

fallback: I’m sorry, I’m not quite sure what happened. I can help with common minor injuries such as cuts, burns, bruises, sprains, nosebleeds, head bumps, splinters, and insect bites. Could you describe the injury in a few simple words? If someone has trouble breathing, is unconscious, is choking, may be poisoned, or bleeding will not stop, call local emergency services now.
